Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the forecasts compared to true outcomes, and how sentiment history relates to these errors.

## Example 1 Analysis (2025-07-16)
History shows prices around 70.40-72.97, generally stable with some variation.
Sentiment: Mostly 0.00, with a few instances of 1.00 (days 9, 11, 12, 15)

Model forecasts: Around 70.28-72.80 range
True outcomes: Around 70.28-72.80 range but specifically:
- The model appears to be too low in some areas and too high in others

Let me look more carefully at the pattern. Looking at the first 10 days of forecasts vs outcomes:

Day 1: Model 71.18 vs True 71.31 (off by -0.13)
Day 2: Model 70.23 vs True 70.55 (off by -0.32)
Day 3: Model 69.49 vs True 69.89 (off by -0.40)
Day 4: Model 69.45 vs True 69.83 (off by -0.38)
Day 5: Model 68.77 vs True 69.11 (off by -0.34)
Day 6: Model 68.88 vs True 69.36 (off by -0.48)
Day 7: Model 70.27 vs True 70.88 (off by -0.61)
Day 8: Model 70.61 vs True 71.34 (off by -0.73)
Day 9: Model 69.93 vs True 70.65 (off by -0.72)
Day 10: Model 72.38 vs True 73.08 (off by -0.70)

The model is consistently under-predicting by about 0.3-0.7 points in the early horizon, and the gap seems to widen slightly.


I notice a potential correlation between model predictions and sentiment. When sentiment shifts from 0.00 to 1.00, the predictions become more aligned with true outcomes. Specifically, days with high sentiment (1.00) show more accurate forecasts, with differences narrowing to around 0.3-0.6 points. This suggests sentiment might be a valuable indicator for refining price predictions.
